cards.text: This psalm is "For the choirmaster. Of David." David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), opens with someone he calls the fool, and the fool is talking. Not out loud, friend, just in his heart, which is about as private as a group chat with your boss in it.

cards.question: The fool says in his heart, "There is no ___."

cards.text: Then David zooms out from one fool to a whole crowd: "They are corrupt; their acts are vile." Friend, I've had burnt batches get better reviews than that.

cards.question: In verse 1, David says there are still a few people out there who do good.

cards.text: Now look up. The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men, scanning everybody, like me going through a whole tray hunting for ONE cookie that came out right.

cards.question: When the LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men, what is He looking for?

answers.text: Anyone who understands and seeks God
Anyone strong enough to fight for Him
Anyone who brings Him the best gifts

cards.question: In verse 3, David says only the fools have turned away, and everyone else is doing fine.

cards.text: All have turned away, and there is no one who does good, "not even one." The expired coupon I shared that junk drawer with believed in EVERYTHING, and even he would've needed to sit down after that line.
Verse 4 asks, "Will the workers of iniquity never learn?" They devour "my people" like bread, and I bet that question comes out through gritted teeth.

cards.question: The workers of iniquity devour "my people" like bread. What else does verse 4 say they refuse to do?

cards.text: But then the whole thing flips: "There they are, overwhelmed with dread." The ones doing all the devouring? Not so tough now.

cards.question: Why are the workers of iniquity overwhelmed with dread?

answers.text: God is in the company of the righteous
A great army is marching toward them
Their own king has turned against them

cards.text: Then the psalm talks right to them: "You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed." Messing up the plans of people who are already being pushed down. That's LOW, friend.

cards.question: The sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, "yet the LORD is their ___."

cards.text: The last verse turns into a longing, a big "Oh, that" moment. David wants the salvation of Israel to come, and he names the place he wants it to come from.

cards.question: "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from ___!"
When the LORD restores His captive people, what does the psalm call Jacob and Israel to do?

cards.text: Captive people restored, Jacob rejoicing, Israel glad. Friend, I know what it's like to sit in the dark waiting on a drawer to open, so when David gets to that line, I'm clapping with my WHOLE mustache.

findings.problem: The joke compares the fool speaking 'in his heart' to 'a group chat with your boss in it,' which is not private at all. The text presents the heart as private, so the comparison works against the fact and leaves the reader asking whether the fool's thought is private or not. The core action (saying something privately) doesn't match the comparison (saying something where the boss can see it).

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The group chat joke doesn't click without explaining. It could imply that God sees the heart, or that the fool's thought is exposed, but neither reading is clear from the line.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank quotes the psalm's line and blanks its last word ('There is no ___.'). The baker has to guess the wording of the line. Card 1 only says the fool is talking in his heart, so nothing lets the baker reason out 'God' over 'king' or 'hope.'

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The question opens with 'In verse 1, David says…', which reads like a test question instead of Papa Dorin pausing mid-passage.

rule.text: Ask from inside the passage, the way a storyteller pauses to let the listener lean in. The question comes out of the moment Papa Dorin just set up.

findings.problem: The question opens with 'In verse 3, David says…', which reads like a test question. It also asks about verse 3 before any story card has set up that moment, so it doesn't come out of a moment Papa Dorin just set up.

rule.text: Ask from inside the passage, the way a storyteller pauses to let the listener lean in. The question comes out of the moment Papa Dorin just set up.

findings.problem: 'What else does verse 4 say they refuse to do?' points to a verse number, like the bad example 'According to verse 17…', and sounds like a test question.

rule.text: The bad ones sound like a test question. The good ones sound like Papa Dorin pausing mid-story.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank quotes the line 'yet the LORD is their ___' and asks the baker to supply its wording (shelter, witness or teacher). This tests the exact word, not the meaning of the verse.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank quotes the psalm's line and blanks its last word ('would come from ___!'), so the baker guesses the wording of the line. Card 15 only says David names a place, with nothing to reason from.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card restates what card 17 just answered (captive people restored, Jacob rejoicing, Israel glad). It adds nothing from the passage and doesn't move the baker forward.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: 'Captive people restored, Jacob rejoicing, Israel glad' states verse 7 as if it has already happened. The text frames it as a longing and a call: 'Oh, that…', 'When the LORD restores…', 'let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!'

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.
